crawler.headline: AI crawler docs shift toward machine-readable indexes, IP verification, and granular opt-out mechanisms.
crawler.body: Over the past year, AI crawler documentation has undergone four interconnected transformations. First, major vendors (OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon) have begun publishing IP-range lists for crawler verification, replacing earlier blanket disclaimers that IPs were unpublished or unreliable—a material improvement for firewall-based detection. Second, new bot identities and UA strings have proliferated (OpenAI's OAI-AdsBot, Amazon's three-bot taxonomy, clarified CCBot URL suffixes), requiring webmasters to update allowlist/blocklist rules; simultaneously, Google renamed its IP-range JSON endpoint from `googlebot.json` to `common-crawlers.json`, signaling a broader IP-range reorganization. Third, page-level and meta-tag opt-out mechanisms have emerged (Amazon's `noarchive` meta tag for training exclusion, Cloudflare's 301-redirect steering for canonical-URL deduplication), layering on top of robots.txt. Fourth, machine-readable site indexes—particularly the `llms.txt` convention—have begun appearing in crawler documentation as a canonical entry point, and Cloudflare's Radar tools now expose adoption metrics and per-crawler response rates across the web. Infrastructure vendors (Cloudflare) have simultaneously expanded their AI-crawl-control offerings with redirect rules, content-format diagnostics, and WAF-rule composition, indicating tighter integration of crawler controls into mainstream CDN/WAF products.

ecosystem.headline: Agent traffic surges as publishers and platforms race to govern scraping and AI access
ecosystem.body: The past month crystallized a structural shift: AI agents are becoming mainstream infrastructure, not edge case, with DataDome reporting 50x surge in Model Context Protocol (MCP) traffic as Anthropic expands connectors. In parallel, publishers escalated legal and technical defenses—the News Media Alliance filed an amicus brief backing Amazon's action against Perplexity, while platforms like Cloudflare and DataDome rolled out gatekeeping tools (Redirects for AI Training, Agent Trust control plane) designed to segment agent access from human traffic. Regulators moved on two fronts: the EU simplified AI rules while explicitly banning nudification tech, and the UK CMA began algorithm scrutiny. The net effect is a hardening ecosystem—publishers demanding scraping restrictions, platforms building triage infrastructure, and regulators standardizing what "responsible AI access" means. Content protection strategies now span legal action, technical redirection, and vendor evaluation frameworks.

agent.headline: Agent infrastructure standardization moves from proprietary to open standards; bot identity frameworks shift from detection to trust protocols.
agent.body: The last 30 days mark a decisive pivot toward formal standardization in AI agent infrastructure. The IETF's publication of the Agent Identity, Trust, and Lifecycle Protocol (AITLP) on April 19 anchored the period, providing a unified framework for agent authentication and autonomous payments across vendors. Simultaneously, OpenAI solidified its own agent stack—deploying workspace agents in ChatGPT, hardening security frameworks, and rolling out Windows sandbox implementations and voice agent integrations—signaling maturation beyond experimentation. Cloudflare's mid-period intervention reframed the entire bot-identity conversation: the industry is abandoning binary "bot vs. human" classification in favor of behavior-based detection and privacy-preserving credential systems like Privacy Pass. This reflects a broader acceptance that agent identity is about trust architecture, not gatekeeping. Early adoption is visible (Sea Limited's engineering deployment, real-world agent standards adoption) but ecosystem consolidation remains incomplete.
